extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and current short-fiction magazine editors/publishers, genre fiction community (authors, readers), and supporters of small magazines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for launching, running, and supporting short-fiction magazines (especially digital-native and aspirant markets), with emphasis on financial viability, quality maintenance, and community support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine business-model classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines can be grouped by how they fund themselves: professionals (fully self-supporting: Analog, Asimov's, F&SF), corporate-supported (e.g., Tor.com, Subterranean), non-profits (e.g., Strange Horizons), hobbyists/beginners (low/no pay), aspirants (pay SFWA-qualifying rates or better but lack sustainable revenue), and conceivables (cover costs but don't adequately compensate staff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to assess where a publication sits in the market and what challenges it will likely face; categories are descriptive of business foundation rather than quality judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial self-sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional magazine completely supports itself from the revenue it generates; aspirants and conceivables often lack this stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether revenue covers operating costs and staff/author compensation; lack of self-sustainability indicates higher risk of closure or untenable compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to market shifts / digital orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful magazines adapt to changes (e.g., the shift from print to digital). Many recent launches are digital-native because digital lowers barriers and costs compared to print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a publication’s model and distribution align with current market realities (digital-first strategies, realistic print commitments); failure to adapt can threaten longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear metric for when to quit
rubrics_metrics.description: New projects need a predefined metric for knowing when to fold (for example, how much money are you willing to lose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the venture as a business, not a baby: define financial thresholds and decision points up front; no shame in folding and trying later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start small and grow with a multi-year plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Map out where you want to be in three years and build toward it gradually rather than trying to be everything immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic, staged goals tied to building readership and revenue; even with initial funding, plan for sustainable growth rather than rapid, unfunded expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on just-in-time funding; build stable revenue streams
rubrics_metrics.description: Just-in-time funding is not a sane or sustainable business model; publications should have predictable income sources (subscriptions, Patreon, parent-company support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage subscription services, patronage platforms, or other reliable income mechanisms; if a magazine lacks them, advise adding such options to improve stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay authors fairly / revisit qualifying payment rates
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues SFWA's qualifying rate for short fiction is too easy to attain given the explosion of markets paying that rate and suggests raising it; authors deserve better compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider author pay as both an ethical and market-quality signal; higher pay can help professionalize markets and attract/retain quality contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clear post-funding sustainability plans for new or revival projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not support new or revival projects until they clearly outline reasonable goals to sustain the publication after their initial funding runs out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: revivals propped up by passion without realistic revenue plans (example: Realms of Fantasy). Vet proposals for long-term viability before backing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain story quality; avoid dilution from overcapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of quality stories isn't growing as fast as the number of slots publishers need to fill, quality will dip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor acceptance standards and publication frequency relative to submission quality; avoid expanding issue sizes or venues beyond what the available pool of high-quality work supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grow and monetize the reader base
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustainability depends on readers willing to pay for short fiction; readership growth must keep pace with publishers' financial needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in reader acquisition and retention (introducing new readers to favorite stories/magazines, marketing, making it easy to subscribe/pay) to ensure a paying audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage community financial support before crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscribers/supporters should back magazines they’d be willing to bail out if they ran aground; support magazines before they need emergency funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should subscribe, donate, or use patron platforms proactively; community support prior to crisis is more sustainable than ad-hoc rescues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer subscriptions and accessible patronage options
rubrics_metrics.description: If a magazine doesn't offer subscriptions or a Patreon-like page, encourage them to add these ways for readers to support financially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making support easy and visible increases the chance of steady revenue; absence of accessible support channels is a solvable vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate compensation for staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Some conceivables cover costs but do not adequately compensate their staff; sustainable publications should aim to pay staff appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider staff compensation when assessing a publication's long-term health and ethical standing; undercompensated staff can lead to burnout and turnover, harming quality and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic acceptance of market correction and attrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Many magazines likely won't be around in a decade; the market corrects itself and new entrants may replace fallen ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan with the expectation of attrition: be realistic about survival odds, focus on sustainable practices, and recognize that market churn is normal.
